chapter_theme: A stretch of sustained description of the mountain where the lion lives: first its perils (cloud, tangle, serpents, bears), then its gem rocks and a long catalogue of flowering trees, ending in lovers' comparisons. No event occurs; it prepares the lion hunt.

cast.role: unnamed speaker who points out the mountain to a hero, inferred from the second-person words in 738, 742 to 744
the unnamed hero addressed (a prince, by inference); 743 calls him broad-chested

735.reading: Cloud banks cover the mountain so thickly that day seems eaten by night, and torrents and seeping wet make the broad slopes impassable.

736.reading: The slope is choked with tangled creepers, cane and bamboo, dark and many-kinded, and is said to be unfit to approach.

737.reading: Great snakes with cave-wide mouths lie sleeping among boulder heaps, having swallowed the elephants that roamed there.

738.reading: The speaker points out hissing snakes, growling beasts and elephant dens, and says these troubles are for all who are not 'ours'.
738.nuance: Whether the hearer is the same hero as in 742 and 743 is inferred; the verse itself only says 'see' (கண்டாய்).

739.reading: Clouds pour flood-water on the groves while the addressee is urged to go swiftly; the sense of the first lines is unclear.

740.reading: Ground that looks sound hides pits or mire where elephants sink beyond saving, while a far glow flickers; the sense is doubtful.

741.reading: Gem-studded rocks give off a glow like many moons, so bright that it dazzles those who look.

742.reading: The speaker tells the hero that, since the seasons do not change here, this mountain can hardly be told apart from the heaven of the scriptures.
742.nuance: The heaven is called by the word for scripture (சுருதி); the verse compares scenery to it and makes no doctrinal claim.

743.reading: Jewel-rocks and stone chambers, mixed with fragrant kongu flowers, shine like old lamps against the sky.

744.reading: A very short, compressed verse addressing a garlanded one with a question about rows or waves; its sense is unsettled.

745.reading: In a word-play verse, mango trees rise on the slope, flowers spread, seepage never dries and the place turns dark as night.

746.reading: In a word-play verse, young women with bangles and their companions pass the time in games in the broad groves.

747.reading: The groves ring with bees and spread with opening flowers, where bangled women play and let petals fall, so that every place looks like their play.

748.reading: Lotus and champak bloom spread over the slope; the fine second half of the verse is hard to parse.

749.reading: A word-play verse on one word (elephant, snake, mountain, tree) describes sandal groves, humming bees, pollen and gem-spitting snakes, and says the place mocks the nagas' own world.

750.reading: The verse lists the flowering trees of the slope, naming nirava, duruka and asoka among them.

751.reading: The list of slope flowers goes on, with kodal, thondri, ingi and maruthu named.

752.reading: Sandal and cool leaf-garlands stand ready for the women of the wild, and the branches hold out blossom garlands.

753.reading: Kinnaras take pleasure here and mandara trees shine; the third line speaks of fear and the fearful.

754.reading: Gold-bright kongu and vengai blooms spread among the rocks, like Indra's bow broken and fallen among dark clouds.

755.reading: Heaps of blue-gem rock are half hidden by fallen blossom, like the hair-knots of women in fire-red cloth.

756.reading: Sun-lit rock slabs strewn with pollen look like the red-cloth beds where young lovers lie.

757.reading: Red ashoka blossom hums with bees against blue rocks, and the sight is compared to youths smeared with saffron paste and adorned.

links.note: Verse 126 has women playing with youths on the Vidyadhara hill until their powder stains the rocks; verse 747 has bangled women at play and petals falling in the lion's mountain.
links.teaches: The poet reuses one pleasure-on-the-hill picture for two different mountains, so the lion's range is painted as a pleasure ground as much as a hunting ground.

links.note: Akananuru 84 sets a rainbow on the mountain under rain clouds as the season of return; verse 754 uses Indra's broken bow among dark clouds only as a likeness for blossom.
links.teaches: The same bow-on-the-hill image works as a season marker in the Sangam poem and as a bare comparison here.

gains.a: The verse lacks any use for the image beyond decoration; the poem shows it can mark a season and a waiting.
gains.b: The poem lacks the Indra's-bow naming that ties the rainbow to a god's weapon, which the verse supplies.

links.note: Akananuru 38 has the ashoka as the lovers' old swing-tree now empty; verse 757 has the ashoka in red pollen and humming bees, likened to adorned youths.
links.teaches: The ashoka stands for young lovers in both, one time in their absence and one time as their likeness.

gains.a: The verse lacks the ashoka's use as a trysting place, which the poem gives.
gains.b: The poem lacks the ashoka's red pollen and the likeness to adorned youths, which the verse gives.

source_issues: Verses 735 to 741, 744 to 749 and 752 to 753: word division and compressed grammar leave the sense uncertain; flagged.
Verses 745 to 749 are word-play (yamaka) verses; readings give only the overall picture.
Verses 738 and 742 to 744 address a hearer; the speaker and hearer are not named and are inferred.
